beats.narration: Begin by framing Pipeline Foundations as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Consider this worked case: A learner maps the inputs, constraints, and observable result for Pipeline Foundations, then checks each step against the stated claim. On screen, show a flowchart with five labeled boxes: Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, Decision Rule. Arrow connects each box sequentially. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart with five labeled boxes: Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, Decision Rule. Arrow connects each box sequentially.

beats.narration: Now define Image Representation precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Consider this worked case: A 100x100 pixel grayscale image becomes a 10000-element array where each value ranges from 0 to 255. On screen, display a small grid of pixel values next to a corresponding numeric array representation. Highlight the mapping between spatial coordinates and array indices. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Image Representation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a small grid of pixel values next to a corresponding numeric array representation. Highlight the mapping between spatial coordinates and array indices.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Color Conversion operates in a concrete sequence. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Consider this worked case: Converting an RGB image to HSV separates color information from brightness, allowing algorithms to isolate specific hues regardless of lighting intensity. On screen, show a side-by-side comparison of an RGB image and its HSV equivalent, with a legend explaining how hue channels isolate color data. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Color Conversion
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison of an RGB image and its HSV equivalent, with a legend explaining how hue channels isolate color data.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Filtering and make the decision criteria explicit. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Consider this worked case: A Gaussian blur filter averages adjacent pixel values to reduce sensor noise and highlight large-scale object boundaries. On screen, display a noisy image, a filtered image, and a sliding window overlay showing how neighboring pixels are averaged. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Filtering
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a noisy image, a filtered image, and a sliding window overlay showing how neighboring pixels are averaged.

beats.narration: Apply Feature Methods to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Consider this worked case: SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) identifies keypoints and generates descriptors that remain consistent across scale and rotation changes. On screen, show an image with detected keypoints marked as circles, connected by lines to corresponding keypoints in a transformed image. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Feature Methods
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show an image with detected keypoints marked as circles, connected by lines to corresponding keypoints in a transformed image.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Calibration, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Consider this worked case: Using a chessboard pattern, the system calculates focal length and principal point to map 2D image coordinates to 3D space accurately. On screen, display a chessboard grid overlaid on a real-world scene, with a diagram showing the projection matrix transforming 2D to 3D coordinates. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Calibration
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a chessboard grid overlaid on a real-world scene, with a diagram showing the projection matrix transforming 2D to 3D coordinates.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Geometric Transforms with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Consider this worked case: Affine transformation adjusts image coordinates to correct perspective distortion in a tilted photograph. On screen, show a distorted image and a corrected image, with a transformation matrix displayed alongside the coordinate mapping lines. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Geometric Transforms
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a distorted image and a corrected image, with a transformation matrix displayed alongside the coordinate mapping lines.

beats.narration: Use Segmentation to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Consider this worked case: Thresholding separates foreground objects from the background by classifying pixels based on intensity values above or below a set level. On screen, display a binary mask where foreground objects are white and background is black, overlaid on the original image. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Segmentation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a binary mask where foreground objects are white and background is black, overlaid on the original image.

beats.narration: Connect Motion Methods to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Motion methods compare observations across time. Consider this worked case: Optical flow calculates pixel displacement between consecutive frames to track object movement and estimate velocity. On screen, show a sequence of three frames with vector arrows indicating pixel movement from frame to frame. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Motion Methods
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a sequence of three frames with vector arrows indicating pixel movement from frame to frame.

beats.narration: Finish with Evaluation & Robustness as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics. Consider this worked case: Varying the threshold value changes the number of detected edges, demonstrating how sensitivity to illumination and noise affects detection accuracy. On screen, display a slider adjusting a threshold value, with corresponding binary masks showing how edge detection changes as the threshold shifts. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Evaluation & Robustness
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a slider adjusting a threshold value, with corresponding binary masks showing how edge detection changes as the threshold shifts.

sources.excerpt: An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments and oral/written summaries of research papers are required. Prerequisites:((CSCI-603 or CSCI-605) &CSCI-661) with grades of B or better or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262)&(CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)).If you have earned credit for CSCI-331 or you are currently enrolled in CSCI-331 you won't be permitted to enroll in CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

sources.excerpt: Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.
